g.text: Population, economy and travel highlights in a single-page overview
Approximate position of Japan’s main islands and four largest metropolitan areas.
Japan: an island nation at the edge of the Pacific

text.tspan: Japan is an archipelago of nearly 7,000 islands in East Asia, stretching
from snowy Hokkaidō in the north to subtropical Okinawa in the south.
Home to more than 120 million people, it combines densely populated
megacities such as Tokyo and Osaka with mountains, forests, and extensive
coastlines shaped by the Pacific “Ring of Fire”.
Japan is the world’s 4th largest economy, a center of high technology,
automotive manufacturing, and pop culture, while maintaining deep
traditions in art, cuisine, and seasonal festivals.

Despite its advanced infrastructure and high life expectancy, Japan faces structural challenges: a rapidly aging population, low birth rates, and exposure to earthquakes and typhoons. At the same time, it remains one of

the safest and most efficient countries in the world, with punctual public transport, strong public services, and a distinctive cultural landscape that ranges from Buddhist temples and Shintō shrines to cutting-edge urban
architecture and design.
Japan’s economy is driven by manufacturing, advanced electronics, automotive exports, and specialised services. After the rapid growth of
the post‑war decades, it has experienced long periods of low inflation and modest real growth, with persistent deflationary pressure and the world’s
highest public debt ratio.
The chart highlights Japan’s nominal GDP in current US dollars. Exchange rate swings can significantly affect dollar‑denominated figures even when
domestic output is relatively stable in yen terms.

Predominantly Japanese, with small foreign communities
Composition of residents by nationality/ethnic grouping (approx., 2023).
From neon skylines to quiet temples

text.tspan: Japan’s compact rail network and high‑speed shinkansen trains make it easy to combine major cities with nature and historic sites.
Tokyo
: world’s largest metropolitan area, with districts like Shibuya,
Shinjuku, and Asakusa, plus museums and contemporary art.
Kyoto
: former imperial capital with thousands of temples and shrines,
including Fushimi Inari’s red torii gates and Kinkaku‑ji’s Golden Pavilion.
Osaka
: known for street food (okonomiyaki, takoyaki), nightlife,
Osaka Castle, and easy access to Nara and Kobe.
Hiroshima & Miyajima
: Peace Memorial Museum and the iconic “floating” torii of
Itsukushima Shrine just a short ferry ride away.
Mount Fuji & Hakone
: Japan’s highest peak, onsen hot springs, lake views,
and classic Fuji silhouettes on clear days.
Hokkaidō
: wide open landscapes, ski resorts like Niseko, lavender
fields in Furano, and fresh seafood in Sapporo and Hakodate.

g.text: Sources: World Bank, IMF World Economic Outlook 2024, Japan Statistics Bureau, JNTO. Values rounded; geographic locations are schematic.
